title: Emit-pace variance field notes: e2e cohort profiling
content:
Purpose and scope:
This is a working note from a short field study where we swept sequence-length cohorts and request patterns to map end-to-end latency percentiles (p50/p95/p99) and produce a per-stage fingerprint for high-variance traces. Goal is to surface actionable hotspots (kernel exec vs batch wait vs kv miss vs egress) and sanity-check our sampling strategy for production SLOs.

Quick summary of what jumped out:
- Two distinct variance regimes: short (<=32 tokens) dominated by small-run kernel overhead + HTTP/egress jitter; long (>=128 tokens) dominated by attention/KV cache churn and batching headroom.
- p99 for mid-range sequences (33-128) is strongly correlated with async-batcher handoffs and rare eviction events.
- A non-negligible fraction (~7%) of p99 traces show high egress serialization time when responses include function-calling metadata (JSON blobs).
- Current trace sampler under-samples cold-KV startups; reweighting by first-token latency improves detection of cold-path regressions.

Experiment setup (notes):
- Hardware: 8xA100 per shard, production kernel build v2.11.0, TFRT-based oppath.
- Workload: production-like mix from route X (chat) and route Y (completion) replayed from 24h traffic; added synthetic single-utterance, multi-utterance bursts to emulate PLG surface.
- Sampling: stratified by seq_len bucket and by user-route; sampled 10k traces per cohort (short/mid/long).
- Measurement: instrumented stage timers at: ingress parse, tokenization, embedding lookup, kv-cache (hit/miss), compile/kernel-exec, async-batcher wait, emit/token-emit loop, post-processing/serde, egress HTTP write.
- Note: kernel exec times exclude syscall/egress overhead; egress measured end-to-end from runtime to customer socket.

Cohort-level percentile table (aggregated):
- short (<=32 tokens): p50=42ms, p95=92ms, p99=210ms, dominant stages=[kernel-exec 35%, egress 22%, tokenize 12%]
- mid (33-128): p50=78ms, p95=240ms, p99=520ms, dominant stages=[async-batcher 33%, kernel-exec 22%, kv-miss 18%]
- long (129-512): p50=260ms, p95=620ms, p99=1.34s, dominant stages=[attention/kernel 48%, kv-cache rehydrate 20%, emit 12%]

Representative trace breakdowns (three examples; times in ms):
- Short p50 example:
  ingress:3, tokenize:7, embed:5, kv-cache(hit):2, kernel-exec:18, emit-loop:4, post-serde:2, egress:3 -> total=44ms
- Mid p95 example (batched wait spike):
  ingress:4, tokenize:10, embed:12, kv-cache(hit):3, batch-wait:130, kernel-exec:65, emit-loop:8, post-serde:5, egress:3 -> total=240ms
- Long p99 example (kv miss + attention stall):
  ingress:6, tokenize:18, embed:25, kv-cache(miss):210 (rehydrate+I/O), kernel-exec/attn:700, emit-loop:60, post-serde:10, egress:5 -> total≈1.73s

Hypotheses and quick verifications run during sweep:
- H1: mid-cohort p99 events are mostly caused by timing alignment with batch boundaries (timeouts + controller backpressure). Quick verify: correlated batch size at request time with p99 probability — Pearson r ~0.57.
- H2: long-cohort p99 often originate from KV cold-paths triggered by session ids with very long contexts. Verified by tagging p99 traces with kv-miss:true -> 68% of long p99 had kv-cache rehydrate events.
- H3: egress/serde accounts for >20% of short-tail p99 when responses exceed 8KB due to JSON heavy metadata. Spot check of top 100 short p99 -> 23 entries had large JSON blobs in function output.

Known instrumentation gaps / caveats:
- We don't currently capture per-kernel GPU queue depth at the time of trace; that makes differentiating kernel contention vs long kernel op times harder.
- Async-batcher telemetry is coarse: we only capture wait time aggregated per-batcher; we should capture per-request enqueue timestamp to attribute head-of-line blocking.
- KV rehydrate includes a variable network call to Vault/cache-store; we currently attribute whole duration to "kv-cache" stage — need to split into local deserialization vs remote retrieval.

Immediate mitigations to try (low effort):
1) Rebalance sampler to include more "first-token" latency samples to catch cold-starts earlier (adjust trace-sampler weight by first_token_ms percentile).
2) Add an egress-size guard for short routes: truncate or stream large function-metadata blobs to reduce serialization stalls.
3) Instrument per-request enqueue times in async-batcher (small PR + 2d infra work) to make head-of-line analysis tractable.
4) For mid-cohort: introduce a jittered batch-flush policy during peak burst windows to reduce alignment spikes (A/B test on a small subset).

Longer-term work (higher effort / cross-team):
- Add GPU-kernel-queue depth telemetry and lightweight sampling of per-op SM utilization (work with infra/runtime kernel team).
- Experiment with KV-prefetch heuristics for long sessions (predictive rehydrate) and measure false-positive rate.
- Revisit serialization path: consider switching default post-serde to stream-based JSON writer for large payloads.

Action items and owners:
- Aisha: open SRV ticket to reweight trace sampler and roll a 2-week capture (done: JIRA SRV-1187).
- Miguel: prototype per-request enqueue timestamps in async-batcher (next sprint).
- Eun-Ji: run a 24h A/B test for jittered batch flush on route X and report p95/p99 deltas.
- Connor: audit function-caller payloads for top 200 short p99 traces and propose streaming changes.

Notes to self / observations:
- Sampling bias matters: naive uniform sampling undercounts rare cold-KV events which are small in total request volume but disproportionately affect p99 SLOs for certain customers.
- Small production change (streaming egress) might buy lots of short-tail SLO improvements with minimal infra cost.
- Maintain a short watch on kernel build v2.11.1 — there are reported micro-optimizations that could reduce small-kernel overheads seen in the short cohort.

Appendix: useful queries and quick scripts
- SQL-ish: SELECT seq_len_bucket, percentile(latency_ms, 50), percentile(latency_ms,95), percentile(latency_ms,99), count(*) FROM traces WHERE route IN (X,Y) AND timestamp > now()-interval '24h' GROUP BY seq_len_bucket;
- grep-like to find kv-miss traces: cat traces-24h.json | jq 'select(.stages.kv_cache.miss==true) | {id:.id, total:.latency_ms, seq_len:.meta.seq_len}' | head -n 200

Next check-in: reconvene after A/B test (Eun-Ji) and async-batcher timestamps draft (Miguel). If jitter test shows >=15% p99 reduction for mid cohort, schedule a rollout plan and instrumentation for canary checks.

Unresolved questions:
- What fraction of customer-visible errors are correlated with these p99 spikes versus independent? Need tighter linking to customer error dashboards.
- Are there specific model families or quantization profiles that amplify the kernel-exec variance? Follow-up profiling on model-variant dimension required.

End of notes.

(Informal style; intended as field notes and handoff — will iterate into a cleaner postmortem if the jitter A/B test surfaces reproducible improvements.)
